foreign.intervention.4.why: Divides internationalist traditions that hold solidarity with foreign revolutions or resistance a duty (Leninist and Trotskyist internationalism, anarchist solidarity, Vietnamese communism, Iranian and Islamist movements, Jacobin fraternity) from sovereigntists, isolationists, realists and order-minded conservatives who see it as meddling. Liberal interventionists and neoconservatives agree only for causes they favour, while paleoconservatives are doctrinally against.

notes.ML: Proletarian internationalism ('Workers of the world, unite') and the Comintern made aid to foreign revolutions a duty: 3.
notes.NLS: Vietnamese communist doctrine and practice of 'nghia vu quoc te' (internationalist duty), including aid to Laos and Cambodia, treats this as a duty: 3.
notes.UJ: Nyerere's Tanzania hosted the OAU Liberation Committee and gave bases to ANC, FRELIMO and others: 3.
notes.VEF: Article 154 of Iran's constitution commits the state to support the struggle of the oppressed against the arrogant everywhere: 3.
notes.JA: The Convention's Decree of Fraternity (November 1792) promised aid to all peoples wishing to recover their liberty: 3.
notes.PA: Buchanan and Taft-style paleoconservatives reject entangling aid to foreign insurgents and the 'democratic crusade': -3.
notes.SDD: Permanent neutrality rules out state military aid to foreign revolutions or resistance: -2.
notes.AC: The CNT-FAI and the international volunteers in Spain (1936) and the anarchist tradition of solidarity make this a duty: 3.
